# History of signalling

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
Explain why signalling developed from local signals to connected systems; distinguish the contributions of block working, interlocking and train detection; recognise the transition from mechanical to electrical and electronic control; and relate older equipment to the principles used today.
:::

## Why study the history?

Many features of current railway signalling have their roots in the origins of the railways as we are still trying to tackle the same problems; keeping trains apart whilst trying to run as many trains as possible. It would be easy to prevent collisions if there was only ever one train on the network at a time, but it wouldn't be very useful.

Having an understanding of how signalling came to be helps to understand why we have the processes and equipment that we do. Many improvements in signalling have come about from accidents, and bearing these in mind helps to understand why it's so important to the safe running of the railway. Some understanding of the history also helps to understand some of the terminology that's used, as some phrases have stuck around since the very beginnings of the railway.

## The first railways

The very first railways of collieries had no need for signalling as they were typically horsedrawn. Even after the opening of the Stockton and Darlington railway in 1825 there was no need for signalling as they initially only had one locomotive. More locomotives were designed and built but there were still very few trains and they were travelling at slow speeds. Providing the trains stuck to the timetable they were generally spaced well apart.

As the railways became busier this stopped being the case. In 1840 a train collision occurred due to trains catching up to each other, and a recommendation was made that drivers should be trained, and that 30 minutes should pass between trains. Mileposts were installed at the side of the railway to allow passengers to report if they felt their train was traveling too fast.

A month later a second accident occurred, where a train stopped at a station was struck by the next train. A new recommendation was made that a red lamp or flag should be displayed for 10 minutes after a train had left a station to prevent the next train departing too closely.

::: trivia
It was around this period that "railway time" was adopted, where all railways should use "London time" instead of their local time. Up until this point the time varied around the country as the sun was the only reliable way of telling the time.
:::

## Local signals and the limits of time

The red lamps and flags used at the very introduction of signalling were quickly replaced with fixed signals. This gave drivers a set location to look for the flags and lamps. It also allowed for better positioning and therefore **signal sighting** than could be achieved by a man at the side of the track.

::: trivia
At the very beginning the men operating these early signals were policemen, which gives rise to signaller's gaining the nickname of "Bobby", which is still occasionally heard today.
:::

Instead of only showing a red flag or light when it was not safe, signals started to show a second "all clear" indication when it was safe to go. What this looked like varied between different railway companies, but eventually this became standardised with the semaphore signal.

![Some examples of early railway signals](https://mysite.du.edu/~etuttle/rail/sigs1.gif){fig-align="center"}

![Semaphore signals
](https://rsme.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Sig-1-1024x853.jpg){fig-align="center"}

The time interval system worked, providing that trains stuck to the timetable. Unfortunately, early trains weren't particularly reliable and often broke down, lost time between stations, or became stuck at an obstruction. Guards were instructed to leave a stopped train and display a danger signal to warn the driver of the following train, but this wasn't a perfect solution.

## Telegraphs and block working

Once invented, the electric telegraph made rapid communication between distant railway locations possible. In 1839, Cooke installed a demonstration telegraph between Paddington and West Drayton, and this enabled a new method of ensuring that trains were kept apart.

![A Glasgow and South Western Railway telegraph instrument](https://content.easyliveauction.com/auctions/images_lots/755D4C38B35FB47DD7BBD80FE725A2EC_gre02/1100065861_PREVIEW.JPG){fig-align="center"}

Communication between distant locations meant that instead of hoping that trains would run to their timetables and keep moving once they'd left a station, it became possible to check that a train had reached its next destination by using telegraphs and bells. This allowed the railway to be divided into sections, or blocks.

The key rule, which remains to this day, became that only one train was allowed in each block section at a time. A second train could not be allowed to enter until the first had been proved to have cleared it.

## Signal boxes and mechanical interlocking

The next major innovation in railway signalling was to be able to remotely control signals and points instead of needing someone to stand at each signal and point to operate them. In 1846 the first signal worked mechanically from a distance was invented. Wires and rodding were attached to each signal and point and brought back to a single location a short distance away where they could be worked by a single signaller.

Bringing all the controls back to a single location also made it possible to safeguard against the signaller being able to set incompatible combinations of signals and point positions. A series of rods and notches were used to prevent levers from physically being pulled to operate signals and points unless it was safe to do so and all the necessary conditions were met.

![Mechanical lever frame and locking tray](https://i.redd.it/kuw9wnohupyd1.jpg){fig-align="center"}

Although mechanical interlockings are becoming less common (and there are none within our section) they are still used, and modern interlockings still apply many of the same principles, just using electrical and electronic methods instead.

### The 1889 legislation

The [Regulation of Railways Act 1889, section 1](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1889/57/pdfs/ukpga_18890057_en.pdf) empowered the Board of Trade to require block working, interlocking of points and signals, and continuous brakes on passenger trains. These were complementary protections: controlling entry to a section, preventing incompatible settings and providing effective braking.

The Act was a major historical step towards wider adoption. It did not invent those protections, nor did it cause every railway to acquire identical equipment on the same date.

## Train detection adds information from the track

Traditional block arrangements depended heavily on observation and communication. Signaller's had to rely on observing the passage of trains themselves, and passing messages about their locations between signal boxes using telegraphs. The invention of train detection in the form of a track circuit allowed confirmation of whether a track circuit was clear to be obtained electrically.

Train detection could be incorporated into signal controls and locking, and automatically prevent signals from being cleared if the track circuit was occupied by a train. Much later, it also allowed automatic signals to respond directly to the state of the track circuit ahead.

For the S&T, this added a new set of interfaces: rails, bonds, insulated joints, ballast, electrical supplies and relays. Decades later, axle counters were introduced which obtained occupation information by counting axles at section boundaries. Both belong to the subject of [train detection](train-detection.qmd), as they perform the same function, although they operate very differently.

## Electrical operation, colour lights and relay logic

Mechanical operation placed practical limits on distances and operating effort. Power-operated points and electrically operated signals allowed the source of operating energy to be located near the equipment. Electrical circuits could carry controls and indications between that equipment and a more distant signal box.

Colour light signals using only lamps instead of semaphore signals were introduced with increasing availability of electricity as these provided better visibility in poor weather conditions.

![Colour light signal at Glasgow Central](https://media-eu.invisioncic.com/y320084/monthly_2023_03/DSCF0006.JPG.4254084d23ba765c4bd170bc856cff83.JPG)

Relays also allowed interlocking conditions to be implemented in circuits instead of mechanical locking trays. A relay contact could represent a required condition, and a combination of contacts could prevent an output unless the designed conditions were satisfied. The safety purpose remained related to that of mechanical locking, although its engineering implementation changed. The combination of many, many relays essentially formed a large computer.

![Example of a relay room. The relays continue for two more rows behind these.](https://live.staticflickr.com/7308/9802794793_b7d99013f1_c.jpg){fig-align="center"}

Panel control and entrance-exit route setting changed the signaller's task. Rather than operating each point and signal separately, the signaller could request a route between two locations. If it was safe to do so, the interlocking would set all the points required and clear the signals.

## Electronic interlocking and signalling centres

The next evolution from relay interlocking was Solid State Interlocking (SSI). This uses electronic equipment and software to perform the same functions as the earlier relays. SSI was introduced later than in other industries due to the complexity of carrying out safety validation of the data and outputs. SSI was first introduced in the mid-1980s.

Remote control and workstation interfaces allowed geographically separated areas to be operated from signalling centres. SSI has enabled the West of Scotland Signalling Centre to control a large area from just one building, rather than multiple different signal boxes.

## Warnings and train protection

Signal sighting had improved and the interlocking could prevent incompatible permissions, but there was still a risk that a driver would not observe and obey all signals. Warning and protection systems were introduced to reduce this risk.

The Automatic Warning System (AWS) was introduced to provide an audible and visual warning of the state of a signal in the driver's cab. If the a warning of a red signal is given and a driver does not acknowledge it the brakes will be automatically applied. The same basic idea idea was first tried in 1906 on the Great Western Railway, but worked differently, with a physical contact between the train and a ramp placed in the four foot. The modern version of AWS uses electromagnets.

![AWS magnet](https://encrypted-tbn0.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcTCIEFfbKfi9-WzYzvdQHv3KaZVS3HZuwQ6sKtA4ONRQhPFXgkKsciVhHY&s=10){fig-align="center"}

AWS begun to be developed in its current form in 1948, and the need for it became more urgent after the [crash at Harrow & Wealdstone in 1952](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow_and_Wealdstone_rail_crash) where it was thought that the driver made no attempt to stop until the last second during fog. AWS was brought into use in 1956. The downside of AWS is that, if a driver acknowledges it, there is nothing stopping them passing a signal at danger. This was the case in the [Bedford train collision in 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Bedford_train_collision).

By 1988 British Rail realised that something was needed that would automatically apply the brakes if a train passed a red signal. Initially they trialed a system known as Automatic Train Protection, which continuously monitors the speed of a train and applies the brakes if it overspeeds or is about to pass a red signal. Two trial installations were installed on the Great Western and Chiltern routes, but it proved too expensive. The Train Protection Warning System (TPWS) was developed as a more affordable alternative which would stop a train that was passing a red signal, but could not continuously monitor the speed throughout a trains whole journey.

TPWS was already being trialled by the time of the [Southall crash in 1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southall_rail_crash) and [Ladbroke Grove crash in 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladbroke_Grove_rail_crash), but these crashes accelerated its roll-out, which began in 2000. Not all signals are fitted with TPWS, with mainly signals around junctions being fitted. It does not prevent trains passing red signals, but tries to prevent any collisions which may occur as a result.
